posts.caption: The dentist's office called at 10:40 asking if I was still coming. I was in the cereal aisle. I had set three alarms for this appointment, one of them labeled DENTIST in all caps, and I swiped every single one away like it was spam. Meanwhile, somewhere in my brain there is a fully preserved jingle for a carpet store that closed decades ago, phone number included. I sang it in the car on the way home. Every word. Perfect pitch. The receptionist was very kind about rescheduling. I wrote the new date on my hand. It's in pen. We'll see.
posts.first: My sister still calls me when she can't remember the words to some commercial from when we were kids. I get it on the first try every time. Last week she asked me what day her own birthday dinner was. I had no idea. We both have our gifts.

posts.caption: A man at the hardware store last Saturday walked me through how to buy a lightbulb. I did not ask. I was holding the lightbulb. He used the tone people use on a puppy that just learned to sit, slow and encouraging, with little pauses so I could keep up. I let him finish, because I was raised right. Then I told him I've been changing my own lightbulbs since 1979 and asked where they keep the extension cords. He pointed. He did not explain the extension cords. Growth is possible for everyone.
posts.first: My husband tried the slow voice once, about twenty years ago, explaining the new remote. I handed him the manual and went to bed. He figured out the remote by himself and never used the voice again. Some lessons only need teaching once.

posts.caption: It arrived in a box bigger than my first apartment. Forty dollars, memory foam, cooling gel, and a little card promising proper cervical alignment, which is a phrase I would have laughed at in 1996. In 1996 I was buying shoes I couldn't walk in to stand at parties I didn't enjoy. Now I read pillow reviews at night the way I used to read magazines. I slept nine hours the first night. Woke up with no neck pain and a level of gratitude usually reserved for weddings. The shoes never did that for me. Not once.
posts.first: My best friend came over Sunday and I made her lie down on the new pillow for a full five minutes before I let her have a glass. She ordered one from my couch. That's what friendship looks like at our age. Product testing.

posts.caption: Tuesday night, a jar of roasted red peppers and I went eleven rounds. I ran it under hot water. I banged the lid on the counter like they do on TV. I tried the rubber glove trick, the spoon trick, and a brief period of prayer. My husband was in the den watching a show about people restoring tractors. I called his name once. He came in, opened it in one twist, said there you go, and was gone before I could say anything clever. It was the most romantic thing that's happened in this house since spring.
posts.first: I've started handing him jars on his way through the kitchen without saying a word. He opens them and hands them back without breaking stride. Twenty-six years of marriage and that is our most efficient system. The dishwasher remains a negotiation.

posts.caption: The blender came home in March with big plans for smoothies. I used it twice. The second time it made a noise like a small plane and leaked purple down the cabinet, and the receipt had long since gone wherever receipts go. A younger me would have driven to the store, stood in the return line, and explained myself to a teenager. Instead it now holds the back door open on nice afternoons, and it is very good at it. Better than it ever was at blending. Everybody finds their calling eventually.
posts.first: There's also a bread maker in the garage that has been a very sturdy plant stand since 2019. My daughter offered to sell it online for me. I told her it already has a job. She didn't argue. She's learning.

posts.caption: Around 8:30 last night I opened the fridge and stood there with the door open like I was waiting for a bus. Same yogurt. Same half lemon. Same leftover lasagna I'd already decided I didn't want. I closed it. Went and sat down. Watched part of a cooking show. Ten minutes later I was back, door open, staring again, as if a small team of grocery elves had come through while my back was turned. They had not. I ate the lasagna. It was fine. It was always going to be the lasagna.
posts.first: My husband does the same thing with the pantry, except he narrates it. We have no snacks, he says. We have four kinds of crackers. He just wants different crackers. I understand him completely and I will never tell him that.

posts.quote: My doctor told me to cut back on stress. So I stopped answering numbers I don't recognize. And numbers I do.
posts.first: Last Thursday I let a call go that turned out to be the pharmacy. Then one from my cousin, the one I actually like. Then a very persistent number from Ohio. I haven't listened to any of the voicemails. I've never slept better, and I'm only a little sorry.

posts.caption: I watched a woman jog past the house at 6 this morning in matching neon, earbuds in, checking her watch like it owed her money. I was on the porch in a sweater I've owned since 1994, holding a coffee that had gone cold an hour ago. I used to be her. Not literally, I never jogged, but I had the watch-checking energy. Every day had to count for something. Somewhere along the way I realized the days count whether you rush them or not. She waved. I waved back. Neither of us stopped what we were doing.
posts.first: My granddaughter asked me last weekend what my goals were for the next five years. I told her to still be sitting in this chair, with this view, in better slippers. She said that wasn't a real goal. I said that's what I thought at your age too.

posts.caption: Saturday was my neighbor's sixtieth, which meant a backyard full of string lights, a playlist heavy on Fleetwood Mac, and at least three people I'd successfully avoided since the last block party. I stayed two hours. I ate the shrimp. I complimented the cake. Then, somewhere around 9:20, I set my glass down on the edge of the patio table, looked at the gate, and simply walked out of it. No announcement. No round of hugs. I was home in my slippers before the candles were lit. She texted Sunday to say what a great time it was. I agreed completely.
posts.first: My husband is the opposite. He says goodbye to every single person, including the dog, and somehow ends up in a twenty-minute conversation by the car about gutters. I've learned to bring a sweater and wait. Marriage is mostly two exit strategies sharing a driveway.

It's in the calendar in blue ink, all day, no details, which makes it look extremely official. What it actually involves is the bathrobe, the good coffee, the crossword, and a long stretch of afternoon where nobody needs anything from me. I haven't had a day like that in about six weeks, and I could feel myself fraying at the edges. Some meetings you don't reschedule. This is one of them.

posts.caption: Last night the remote slid off the arm of my chair and landed on the rug, maybe eighteen inches away. I started the trip. I really did. I leaned forward, got about halfway, heard something in my lower back make a small, polite comment, and stopped there to think it over. The remote looked fine where it was. It was on a channel I liked. I sat back and watched the rest of the show without it. My husband found it Sunday morning and handed it to me like he'd rescued it from a well. It had been perfectly happy down there.

posts.caption: Gave a friend a ride to lunch on Monday and watched her face as she opened the passenger door. There's a beach towel back there from the Fourth of July. A pumpkin spice cup from two weeks ago. A library book I'm now pretty sure I owe money on, three hair ties, one shoe that isn't mine, and a birthday card I meant to mail in August. She moved a bag of returns so she could sit down. I told her to think of it like a museum. Everything has a story. Most of them end with I'll deal with it this weekend.
posts.first: I did clean out the cup holder this morning. Found a quarter, two peppermints, and the earring I accused my husband of losing in the spring. I've decided not to bring that up. Some history is better left in the car.
